query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the selected high‐entropy alloy, superconductivity at low temperature emerges because the high configurational entropy (i.e., the random distribution of five or more elements on a simple lattice) preserves a robust, isotropic s‐wave electron–phonon coupling by stabilizing the local electronic density-of-states. If this disorder is intentionally reduced, the superconducting pairing is expected to be weakened or occur at a lower Tc.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, fully random high-entropy alloy (e.g., a bcc (TaNb)–based or similar HEA where the elements are in near‐equiatomic ratios) whose superconducting behavior at low temperature has not yet been characterized.
generation.intervention: Prepare a controlled variant of the HEA by reducing its configurational entropy – for example, by inducing mild elemental segregation (or by using a slightly non‐equiatomic composition within the solubility limits) that leads to partial short‐range ordering while keeping the overall stoichiometry approximately constant.
generation.conditions: Both the high-entropy (fully disordered) and modified (reduced-entropy) samples are processed identically aside from the intervention; they are tested under the same low-temperature regime (below ~10 K) and ambient pressure, with identical measurement protocols (electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility).
generation.structural_mediator: The local atomic configuration – specifically the degree of short-range disorder versus ordering – which controls the electronic density-of-states at the Fermi level and the effective electron–phonon coupling.
generation.mechanism: A high mixing entropy generates extensive atomic-scale disorder that prevents the formation of localized electronic states or competing orders, thereby stabilizing isotropic s-wave pairing via a stable electron–phonon interaction. By reducing this disorder (i.e., lowering ΔSmix), the density-of-states at the Fermi level is altered and the electron–phonon coupling becomes less effective in inducing superconductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the high-entropy control sample, the HEA variant with reduced configurational entropy will display a lower superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and/or a reduced superconducting volume fraction (i.e. a less well-defined zero-resistance state).
generation.baseline: The fully disordered HEA, as synthesized, exhibits a superconducting transition at a given Tc in the low-temperature regime (e.g., around 7–10 K, as typical for known HEA superconductors).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEAs with similar simple (e.g., bcc) crystal structures and over the low-temperature range where conventional (bulk-like) s-wave superconductivity can form, assuming no extraneous phases or drastic changes in carrier concentration intervene.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the Tc reduction and extent of superconducting property change is uncertain, as additional factors (such as minor variations in carrier concentration or lattice strain) might also play a role.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two series of samples: one series with full equiatomic (maximal configurational entropy) HEA processing and one series with controlled reduction of configurational entropy achieved via slight compositional modulation or post-synthesis thermal treatment that induces partial atomic ordering. Measure the superconducting transition using both four-probe resistivity and magnetic susceptibility under identical low-temperature conditions.
measurements: Electrical resistivity as a function of temperature (to determine the onset and width of the zero-resistance state)
Magnetic susceptibility measurements (to assess bulk superconducting volume fraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA sample with lower configurational entropy does not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in Tc and/or superconducting volume fraction compared to the fully disordered (high-entropy) control – or if its superconductivity is instead enhanced – the proposed mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy-alloy (HEA) superconductors are a new class of disordered superconductors. However, commonality of superconducting characteristics of HEA materials is unclear. Here, we have investigated the crystal and electronic structure, and the robustness of superconducting states in a HEA-type metal telluride (MTe; M = Ag, In, Sn, Pb, Bi) under high pressure, and the results were compared with the pressure effects for a middle-entropy system (AgPbBiTe3) and a reference system of PbTe. When the crystal structure is CsCl-type, all phases show superconductivity under high pressure but exhibit different pressure dependences of the transition temperature (Tc). For PbTe, its Tc decreases with pressure. In contrast, the Tc of HEA-type AgInSnPbBiTe5 is almost independent of pressure, for pressures ranging from 13.0 to 35.1 GPa. Those results suggest that the robustness of superconductivity to external pressure is linked to the configurational entropy of mixing at the M site in MTe. We have experimentally studied the superconducting state of the HEA (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x In thin film form with x=0.35 and x=0.71 by measuring Hc1(T) and Hc2(T). Our analysis of λ(T) is in quantitative agreement with the BCS theory of an isotropic single band s-wave superconductor in the weak coupling limit. The analysis of ξ(T) reveals a comparable amount of disorder at both compositions, lx=0.35≈lx=0.71. Therefore, we can exclude that the observed variations in Tc originate from a disorder-driven mechanism. Further theoretical and experimental studies will be needed to characterize the low-energy electronic structure at various alloy compositions and its influence on Tc. Looking ahead, results of such efforts may inform pathways for realizing HEAs with enhanced superconducting Tc. Employing penetration-depth measurements to other superconducting HEAs, such as those crystallizing on the CsCl-type lattice, it will be interesting to test whether weak coupling s-wave superconductivity is a common occurrence in these material systems.
